title: Find Product Recommendation Pairs
statement:
A shop wants to recommend products that the same customers tend to buy together, using two tables:

- `ProductPurchases(user_id, product_id, quantity)`: a user bought a product, in some positive `quantity`; `(user_id, product_id)` is unique, and every `product_id` exists in `ProductInfo`.
- `ProductInfo(product_id, category, price)`: `product_id` is unique; each product has one `category` and a `price`.

Look at every pair of different products with the smaller id first. Its `customer_count` is the number of distinct users who bought **both** products (quantities do not matter). Report the pairs with `customer_count` of at least 3, with the columns `product1_id` (the smaller id), `product2_id` (the larger id), `product1_category`, `product2_category` and `customer_count`.

Order the rows by `customer_count` descending, then `product1_id` ascending, then `product2_id` ascending.
reference:
WITH pairs AS (
  SELECT a.product_id AS product1_id,
         b.product_id AS product2_id,
         COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS customer_count
  FROM ProductPurchases AS a
  JOIN ProductPurchases AS b
    ON b.user_id = a.user_id
   AND b.product_id > a.product_id
  GROUP BY a.product_id, b.product_id
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) >= 3
)
SELECT p.product1_id,
       p.product2_id,
       i1.category AS product1_category,
       i2.category AS product2_category,
       p.customer_count
FROM pairs AS p
JOIN ProductInfo AS i1
  ON i1.product_id = p.product1_id
JOIN ProductInfo AS i2
  ON i2.product_id = p.product2_id
ORDER BY p.customer_count DESC, p.product1_id, p.product2_id;
brute:
SELECT counted.product1_id, counted.product2_id, counted.product1_category, counted.product2_category, counted.customer_count
FROM (
  SELECT x.product_id AS product1_id,
         y.product_id AS product2_id,
         x.category AS product1_category,
         y.category AS product2_category,
         (SELECT COUNT(*)
          FROM ProductPurchases AS u
          WHERE u.product_id = x.product_id
            AND u.user_id IN (SELECT v.user_id FROM ProductPurchases AS v WHERE v.product_id = y.product_id)) AS customer_count
  FROM ProductInfo AS x, ProductInfo AS y
  WHERE x.product_id < y.product_id
) AS counted
WHERE counted.customer_count >= 3
ORDER BY counted.customer_count DESC, counted.product1_id, counted.product2_id
notes:
## Intuition

A pair of products is "bought together" by a user when that user has a purchase row for each of them. Joining `ProductPurchases` to itself on `user_id` puts every two purchases of the same user side by side, and requiring the second id to be larger keeps each unordered pair exactly once. Grouping those joined rows by the two product ids then counts the users behind each pair; categories are looked up afterwards for the pairs that survive.

## Approach

1. `pairs`: self-join purchases `a` and `b` on the same `user_id` with `b.product_id > a.product_id`, so each user contributes one row per pair of products they bought.
2. Group by the two ids, count distinct users as `customer_count`, and keep groups with `HAVING ... >= 3`.
3. Join `ProductInfo` twice, as `i1` for the first product and `i2` for the second, to fetch both categories.
4. Order by `customer_count` descending, then the two ids ascending.

## Example 1, step by step

- User 1 bought 101, 102, 103: pairs (101, 102), (101, 103), (102, 103).
- User 2: (101, 102), (101, 104), (102, 104). User 3: (101, 103), (101, 105), (103, 105).
- User 4 bought four products, giving six pairs, among them (101, 102), (101, 103) and (102, 104). User 5: (102, 104).
- Counting: (101, 102) has users 1, 2, 4; (101, 103) has 1, 3, 4; (102, 104) has 2, 4, 5. Every other pair has at most 2 users and is dropped.
- All three survivors have count 3, so the smaller `product1_id` comes first, and the smaller `product2_id` breaks what remains: (101, 102) Electronics/Books, (101, 103) Electronics/Clothing, (102, 104) Books/Kitchen.

## Complexity

- Time: O(Σ kᵤ²) for the self-join, where kᵤ is the number of products user u bought, plus sorting the pairs.
- Space: O(number of distinct co-purchased pairs) for the grouping.

## Pitfalls

- Joining on `b.product_id <> a.product_id` lists every pair twice, as (x, y) and (y, x).
- Summing `quantity` instead of counting users: buying five copies is still one customer.
- Using `> 3` instead of `>= 3` loses pairs bought by exactly three customers.
- Forgetting the tie-breaks: equal counts must fall back to `product1_id`, then `product2_id`.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `a`, `b` | two purchases by the same user, `b` of the larger product id |
| `pairs` | one row per product pair with its `customer_count`, at least 3 |
| `p` | `pairs` in the final query |
| `i1`, `i2` | `ProductInfo` rows of the first and second product |

narration.1: The pairs stage counts, for every product pair, how many users bought both products.
narration.4: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts customers, not quantities or purchase rows.
narration.6: Joining purchases to themselves places two purchases side by side.
narration.7: Both purchases must belong to the same user.
narration.8: Requiring the larger id on the right keeps each unordered pair once, smaller id first.
narration.9: Grouping by the two ids gives one row per pair.
narration.10: Only pairs bought by at least three different customers are recommendations.
narration.17: The final query starts from the pairs that passed the threshold.
narration.18: The first product's row of ProductInfo supplies product1_category.
narration.20: A second copy of ProductInfo supplies product2_category.
narration.22: Most-shared pairs come first; ties fall back to the smaller product ids.
